## Objective

Define and deliver `{trinity}` as a local-first candidate processing workflow platform that transforms raw evidence into ranked, decision-ready outputs for downstream products such as `{reply}`.

## Unified Context

The system we are building is not a single reply assistant and not a single benchmark. It is a reusable runtime workflow built around a fixed sequence:

- ingest evidence,
- generate candidates,
- refine candidates,
- evaluate candidates,
- surface the frontier,
- learn from feedback.

This repository exists to build that runtime workflow cleanly and locally first. It must stay distinct from `{train}`:

- `{trinity}` runs the workflow,
- `{train}` improves parts of the workflow through bounded optimization.

The likely first embedding is `{reply}`, where one contact timeline and one composer can consume the workflow to draft strong next messages. But the platform must remain broad enough to support other brains later, such as domain tutors, knowledge assistants, and advisory systems.

## Problem

Without one canonical roadmap issue:

- the repository can drift into a product-specific implementation,
- runtime workflow concerns can get mixed with optimizer concerns from `{train}`,
- local-first requirements can get weakened by convenience shortcuts,
- future contributors will not know what the true product boundary is.

## Goal

Create one roadmap anchor that defines `{trinity}` as the reusable local-first runtime workflow layer, with a clear distinction from `{train}` and with enough structure to ship a first production embedding.

## Scope
### In Scope

- define `{trinity}` as a reusable workflow runtime
- define the distinction between workflow, memory, product adapters, model adapters, and operator apps
- define the local-first development posture
- sequence the work needed for the first usable workflow MVP
- keep the first `{reply}` embedding explicit without letting it define the whole platform

### Out of Scope

- implementing every future product adapter immediately
- turning the roadmap into a vague abstract research program
- moving optimization logic from `{train}` into `{trinity}` core

## Execution Prompt

Treat this issue as the delivery anchor for the whole repository. The platform must be local-first in reality, reusable in design, and still narrow enough to produce a real working workflow proof.

## Constraints

- `{trinity}` must remain distinct from `{train}`
- the workflow stages must be explicit, not implied by prompt glue
- the platform must support multilingual and multi-domain use later without overfitting to one product now
- operator and product surfaces must consume runtime contracts rather than redefine them
- repository standards must live in-repo, not in private discussion only

## Acceptance Checks

- the roadmap clearly defines `{trinity}` as a reusable local-first workflow runtime
- the separation from `{train}` is explicit
- downstream issues separate workflow, memory, model, product, and app concerns
- the board is immediately usable as a delivery plan

## Dependencies

- None yet. This is the planning anchor.

## Risks

- If the roadmap becomes `{reply}`-specific, future reuse will be expensive
- If the roadmap becomes abstract-first, the repository will stall before a real proof exists
- If `{trinity}` and `{train}` are conflated, both platforms will become harder to reason about

## Delivery Artifact

A board-centered roadmap issue that defines `{trinity}` as a reusable local-first candidate processing workflow platform.

## Developer Notes

This issue should remain the top-level planning anchor until the workflow boundaries are stable enough to support multiple product embeddings and an explicit optimization seam into `{train}`.

## Objective

Establish the repository bootstrap, operating docs, coding standards, definition of done, design system baseline, and macOS-first development scaffold for `{trinity}`.

## Unified Context

Before workflow code can be built responsibly, the repository needs a durable operating contract. `{trinity}` is intended to become a long-lived local-first runtime platform, so contributors and agents need a stable place to start: documentation, folder structure, development expectations, and a buildable native shell.

The current implementation baseline now includes:

- repository bootstrap files
- SSOT documentation under `docs/`
- a Python tooling scaffold
- a minimal SwiftUI macOS shell under `apps/macos`
- verification through `uv run pytest`, `uv run ruff check .`, and `swift build`

That means this issue is no longer hypothetical bootstrap work. It now serves as the formal record of the delivered starting point.

## Problem

Without a repository and development baseline:

- the workflow contract will be implemented on shifting ground,
- future issues will depend on private assumptions,
- the macOS app work will begin without native conventions,
- handoff quality will degrade immediately.

## Goal

Lock the initial repository contract and development baseline so future implementation work can move through explicit issues instead of renegotiating structure.

## Scope
### In Scope

- README and operating documentation
- coding standards and definition of done
- design system baseline for the operator shell
- macOS development guidance
- minimal SwiftUI shell scaffold
- Python workspace scaffold and smoke test
- handover and status documentation

### Out of Scope

- real workflow execution
- real product adapters
- real persistence or feedback logic

## Execution Prompt

Make the bootstrap strict, public-quality, and immediately usable by a new developer or coding agent.

## Constraints

- the baseline must preserve the distinction between runtime workflow and optimizer work
- the macOS shell must stay thin at this stage
- docs must be public-quality and not internal shorthand
- the repository must be left in a resumable state

## Acceptance Checks

- the repo contains a documented operating model and repository contract
- coding standards and definition of done are explicit
- the repo includes a buildable native shell scaffold
- the repo includes a minimal Python tooling path
- `README.md`, `docs/STATUS.md`, and `docs/HANDOVER.md` are ready for handoff

## Dependencies

- #1

## Risks

- Weak bootstrap quality will create recurring ambiguity on every later issue
- If the shell grows too early, app code will absorb workflow logic prematurely

## Delivery Artifact

A bootstrapped `{trinity}` repository ready for real implementation work.

## Developer Notes

This issue is expected to close early and remain the reference point for how the repo was intentionally initialized.

## Objective

Define and implement the core evidence ingestion contract for `{trinity}`, including canonicalization, deduplication, provenance, timestamping, and tenant-bound lifecycle rules.

## Unified Context

The workflow starts with evidence. If the evidence layer is unstable, every later stage inherits noise, duplication, and false confidence. `{trinity}` is intended to process omnichannel input such as messages, notes, and domain evidence under one common runtime contract, so the evidence model must be explicit and reusable.

The formal spec already points toward an `EvidenceUnit` model with canonical content, source identity, metadata, freshness, and provenance. This issue turns that conceptual contract into implementation-ready runtime behavior.

## Problem

Without a strict ingestion contract:

- duplicate evidence will distort downstream generation and evaluation,
- provenance will be too weak for debugging and trust,
- source-specific hacks will leak into later stages,
- local product adapters such as `{reply}` will have no stable ingestion seam.

## Goal

Build the first durable evidence contract so every later stage can trust what “evidence” means in the system.

## Scope
### In Scope

- `EvidenceUnit` schema
- canonicalization rules for stable hashing and comparison
- exact-hash deduplication rules
- source type and source reference contracts
- provenance and freshness fields
- tenant-bound write rules
- deterministic tests for ingestion behavior

### Out of Scope

- full product adapter integration
- candidate generation
- feedback learning
- UI implementation beyond developer visibility needs

## Execution Prompt

Treat ingestion as a trust boundary. The point is to create stable, auditable runtime input, not just to get bytes into a database.

## Constraints

- canonicalization must be deterministic
- provenance must be retained explicitly
- all writes must remain tenant-bound
- ingestion must be reusable across products and not shaped only around `{reply}`
- malformed evidence must fail closed or be surfaced explicitly

## Acceptance Checks

- the system has an explicit `EvidenceUnit` contract
- canonical content hashing is stable
- exact duplicates are rejected or suppressed deterministically
- provenance is durable enough for audit and debugging
- tests cover canonicalization, deduplication, and source metadata behavior

## Dependencies

- #1
- #2

## Risks

- Weak ingestion contracts will create silent corruption in later stages
- Overfitting the schema to one product source will reduce platform reuse

## Delivery Artifact

A machine-checkable evidence ingestion and provenance contract for `{trinity}`.

## Developer Notes

This issue is upstream of generation, refinement, evaluation, and feedback. Keep it explicit and product-neutral.

## Objective

Define and implement the candidate lifecycle contract that governs how `{trinity}` represents generated, refined, evaluated, suppressed, reworked, archived, and delivered candidates.

## Unified Context

`{trinity}` exists to turn evidence into decision-ready outputs. The bridge between raw evidence and surfaced results is the candidate model. The formal workflow already implies candidate states such as `GENERATED`, `REFINED`, `EVALUATED`, `REWORK`, `SUPPRESSED`, `ARCHIVED`, and `DELIVERED`. That lifecycle must become a real contract before execution code or UI code starts improvising.

## Problem

Without a candidate lifecycle schema:

- generator, refiner, evaluator, and frontier logic will produce incompatible objects,
- later auditing will be weak,
- feedback and delivery semantics will not line up cleanly,
- the app surface will be forced to guess state instead of consuming it.

## Goal

Create one durable lifecycle schema for candidates so all runtime stages and app surfaces speak the same language.

## Scope
### In Scope

- candidate base schema
- candidate type rules such as `KNOWLEDGE` and `ACTION`
- state transition semantics
- version-family identity and lineage metadata
- scoring fields such as confidence and ranking inputs
- delivery-only fields where appropriate
- deterministic tests for legal and illegal transitions

### Out of Scope

- actual model execution
- persistence engine selection beyond what is needed for the schema contract
- product-specific rendering behavior

## Execution Prompt

Make the lifecycle boring and explicit. Later sophistication should come from better execution and ranking, not from implicit state changes.

## Constraints

- state transitions must be explicit and testable
- lineage must be preserved across rework and refinement
- delivery semantics must not be over-generalized into every state
- the schema must be usable by both knowledge-style and action-style candidates

## Acceptance Checks

- `{trinity}` has a stable candidate schema and lifecycle vocabulary
- legal transitions are explicit
- illegal transitions fail closed or are surfaced clearly
- candidate lineage can be tracked through refinement and rework
- the contract is documented and covered by tests

## Dependencies

- #1
- #2
- #3

## Risks

- If lifecycle semantics are implicit, debugging the runtime later will be far harder
- Overly UI-shaped lifecycle semantics will make core runtime reuse harder

## Delivery Artifact

A runtime-level candidate lifecycle contract for `{trinity}`.

## Developer Notes

This issue is the seam between evidence processing and surfaced frontier behavior. Keep the seam strict.

## Objective

Implement the execution contract for the three core processing stages in `{trinity}`: generator, refiner, and evaluator.

## Unified Context

The central workflow of `{trinity}` is staged on purpose. Generation should maximize useful recall, refinement should improve clarity and structure, and evaluation should score candidates under explicit policy. Those stages must exist as real runtime seams rather than one blended prompt chain.

This issue is where the workflow becomes executable in a disciplined way.

## Problem

Without an explicit execution contract:

- stage boundaries will blur,
- candidate quality failures will be harder to localize,
- future optimization by `{train}` will not know what component it is improving,
- local model adapter work will leak into workflow logic.

## Goal

Create a stage-oriented runtime contract that can execute generation, refinement, and evaluation separately while preserving shared schemas and auditability.

## Scope
### In Scope

- stage input and output contracts
- orchestration between generator, refiner, and evaluator
- bounded execution semantics per stage
- normalization of raw stage outputs into runtime schemas
- explicit error handling and partial-failure behavior
- tests for stage wiring and failure surfaces

### Out of Scope

- final frontier ranking and suppression policy
- full product adapter integration
- long-term learning and feedback replay

## Execution Prompt

Do not build “prompt soup.” Build stage contracts that can later be inspected, swapped, and optimized independently.

## Constraints

- stage boundaries must remain explicit
- workflow code must stay distinct from model-backend code
- normalized output contracts must be deterministic enough for later evaluation and storage
- failures in one stage must not silently masquerade as valid downstream work

## Acceptance Checks

- the runtime can execute generator, refiner, and evaluator as distinct stages
- raw stage output is normalized into candidate schemas
- stage failures are surfaced explicitly
- the execution contract is documented and testable
- the resulting seams are usable later by `{train}` for optimization work

## Dependencies

- #1
- #3
- #4

## Risks

- A collapsed stage model will make later evaluation and optimization brittle
- If model-specific assumptions leak into stage logic, backend portability will suffer

## Delivery Artifact

A real stage-execution contract for generation, refinement, and evaluation in `{trinity}`.

## Developer Notes

This issue is the workflow core. Keep it inspectable, bounded, and separable.

## Objective

Build the runtime logic that turns evaluated candidates into a small, high-signal frontier suitable for operator review or product delivery.

## Unified Context

`{trinity}` succeeds when the surfaced result set is small, useful, current, and trustworthy. The formal workflow already implies that many internal candidates may exist while the surfaced frontier should remain small. That means frontier selection is not just sorting by one number. It needs suppression, merge, deduplication, and ranking semantics that preserve usefulness while reducing overwhelm.

## Problem

Without explicit frontier logic:

- the operator or product will see too many low-signal candidates,
- the system will repeat itself across near-duplicates,
- feedback will be noisy because the surfaced set will not be curated tightly,
- production embeddings will have no trustworthy “best current options” contract.

## Goal

Define and implement the transformation from evaluated candidate inventory into a small, ranked, actionable frontier.

## Scope
### In Scope

- frontier cardinality rules
- suppression semantics
- merge semantics for overlapping candidates
- ranking rules and tie-breaking
- recency and freshness handling where appropriate
- tests for frontier population behavior

### Out of Scope

- model generation itself
- product-specific UI rendering
- long-term feedback learning beyond the signals needed for frontier behavior

## Execution Prompt

Optimize for operator usefulness, not for showing the system’s work. The system should do the curation internally before asking for human attention.

## Constraints

- the frontier must stay intentionally small
- valid candidate availability should prevent an empty frontier unless policy requires abstention
- suppression and merge decisions must be auditable
- ranking must be explicit enough to debug later

## Acceptance Checks

- the runtime can produce a non-empty frontier from valid evaluated candidates
- near-duplicates can be merged or suppressed deterministically
- ranking and tie-breaking are explicit
- frontier behavior is covered by tests and documented clearly

## Dependencies

- #4
- #5

## Risks

- weak frontier rules will cause operator overload and lower trust
- hidden suppression logic will make production debugging difficult

## Delivery Artifact

A runtime frontier-selection contract for `{trinity}`.

## Developer Notes

This issue defines what the operator actually sees. Treat it as a product-quality trust boundary.

## Objective

Capture user feedback and operational outcomes as durable feedback events that can improve future runtime behavior and later be replayed for analysis or optimization.

## Unified Context

`{trinity}` is not complete when it can only surface candidates. It must also learn from what the operator actually does. In the first `{reply}` embedding, that means actions such as sent unchanged, lightly edited then sent, heavily rewritten, discarded, or marked bad. Those outcomes need a real runtime contract, not ad hoc logging.

## Problem

Without feedback-event capture:

- the system will not improve from real operator behavior,
- “good” and “bad” outcomes will remain private intuition,
- replay for evaluation and later `{train}` optimization will be far weaker,
- product embeddings will treat feedback as a UI event instead of a workflow signal.

## Goal

Create a durable feedback-event and memory contract that lets `{trinity}` learn from usage and gives `{train}` a future path to optimize against real outcomes.

## Scope
### In Scope

- feedback-event schema
- outcome taxonomy
- event linkage to candidates, frontier, and delivered actions
- memory update seams
- replayability requirements for offline analysis
- deterministic tests for event capture and lineage

### Out of Scope

- full machine-learning optimization in this repository
- product-side analytics dashboards beyond what is needed for workflow integrity

## Execution Prompt

Treat feedback as part of the workflow contract, not as optional telemetry.

## Constraints

- feedback events must be durable and traceable
- the contract must support both explicit and inferred signals
- event linkage back to candidate lineage must be preserved
- the design must remain reusable outside `{reply}` even if `{reply}` is the first embedding

## Acceptance Checks

- `{trinity}` has an explicit feedback-event schema
- candidate and frontier outcomes can be recorded durably
- replayable linkage exists from surfaced candidate to resulting feedback event
- the contract is documented and covered by tests

## Dependencies

- #4
- #5
- #6

## Risks

- weak feedback lineage will cripple later optimization and diagnosis
- overfitting the taxonomy to one product UI will limit reuse

## Delivery Artifact

A durable feedback-event memory and replay contract for `{trinity}`.

## Developer Notes

This issue is where runtime behavior becomes learnable instead of merely generative.

## Objective

Build the local persistence and orchestration layer that stores evidence, candidates, feedback, and cycle runs with tenant-bound auditability.

## Unified Context

The formal workflow describes company-level cycles, locks, ingestion, stage processing, maintenance, and frontier recomputation. That requires durable local state. `{trinity}` is local-first, so its first persistence layer must be local, inspectable, and explicit. The system must also preserve lineage across cycle runs for debugging, trust, and future optimization.

## Problem

Without local persistence and cycle orchestration:

- the workflow will not be resumable,
- auditability will be weak,
- company or contact boundaries will be harder to preserve,
- the macOS shell will have no stable source of truth.

## Goal

Implement the first durable local state layer and orchestration semantics for `{trinity}` cycles.

## Scope
### In Scope

- local persistence contract
- tenant-bound write model
- cycle run identity and lineage
- mutual exclusion or lock semantics where needed
- audit-visible records for evidence, candidates, feedback, and frontier state
- tests for orchestration and storage contracts

### Out of Scope

- distributed orchestration
- hosted multi-tenant infrastructure
- product-specific sync protocols beyond what is needed for the local-first core

## Execution Prompt

Build a boring local state layer that is easy to inspect and hard to misunderstand.

## Constraints

- local-first must be the default implementation path
- writes must remain tenant-bound
- cycle-run identity must be durable enough for replay and audit
- the state layer must serve both runtime logic and the macOS shell without duplicating contracts

## Acceptance Checks

- the system has a local persistence contract for core runtime entities
- cycle runs are durable and traceable
- locking or mutual exclusion semantics are explicit where needed
- the macOS shell can read state without re-deriving workflow behavior
- tests cover core orchestration and storage behavior

## Dependencies

- #3
- #4
- #5
- #6
- #7

## Risks

- weak state lineage will make debugging and trust much harder
- mixing app state and runtime state too early will make the system brittle

## Delivery Artifact

A local-first persistence and orchestration baseline for `{trinity}`.

## Developer Notes

This issue is about durable runtime truth, not convenience caching.

## Objective

Add a clean local model adapter layer so `{trinity}` can run embeddings, candidate generation, refinement support, and reranking locally from day one.

## Unified Context

The platform is explicitly local-first. That means local model usage cannot be an optional late add-on if the first production embedding depends on draft generation and ranking. At the same time, model-backend specifics must not leak into workflow logic.

This issue establishes the boundary between:

- workflow stages that need model capabilities,
- model adapters that provide those capabilities locally.

## Problem

Without a model adapter layer:

- local-first claims will remain superficial,
- workflow code will absorb backend-specific assumptions,
- future model swaps will be expensive,
- the first `{reply}` embedding will not have a stable local inference path.

## Goal

Create a model adapter layer for local embeddings, candidate generation, and reranking while keeping the workflow contract independent from any one local runtime.

## Scope
### In Scope

- model adapter interfaces
- local embedding path
- local generation path
- local reranking or evaluation-support path
- explicit capability discovery or configuration contracts
- documentation of local runtime assumptions

### Out of Scope

- supporting every model runtime immediately
- hosted inference as a default path
- product-specific prompt policies

## Execution Prompt

Keep local inference real, but isolate it cleanly. The workflow should depend on capabilities, not on one backend’s quirks.

## Constraints

- local-first is mandatory
- model adapters must stay separate from workflow stages
- the contract must support multilingual use later
- backend quirks must be isolated explicitly

## Acceptance Checks

- `{trinity}` has a documented local model adapter interface
- the workflow can call local embedding, generation, and reranking through that interface
- configuration and capability assumptions are explicit
- model-specific behavior is kept out of workflow core

## Dependencies

- #5
- #8

## Risks

- backend leakage into core workflow will make future changes expensive
- pretending to be local-first while depending on hosted shortcuts will break the product direction

## Delivery Artifact

A local model adapter layer for core `{trinity}` workflow stages.

## Developer Notes

This issue should make “full local from day one” real without letting backend details shape the platform core.

## Objective

Build the first real macOS operator shell that exposes timeline context, frontier candidates, candidate review, and feedback capture on top of the `{trinity}` runtime.

## Unified Context

The first production surface is macOS-first. The shell must let an operator inspect evidence context, review the surfaced frontier, understand provenance and confidence, and feed real outcomes back into the system. It is not supposed to become a second runtime engine; it is an operator surface over runtime contracts.

The repository already includes a minimal SwiftUI scaffold. This issue turns that scaffold into the first useful native workflow.

## Problem

Without an operator shell:

- the runtime will be difficult to inspect and trust,
- feedback capture will stay theoretical,
- local-first product use will be blocked,
- downstream product integration decisions will be made without a native reference surface.

## Goal

Build the first useful native operator experience for `{trinity}` on macOS.

## Scope
### In Scope

- timeline and evidence context view
- frontier list and detail view
- candidate comparison and provenance visibility
- feedback capture surface
- status and cycle visibility where needed for operator trust

### Out of Scope

- full production `{reply}` embedding inside this issue
- hidden workflow logic inside view code
- hosted web-first replacement for the native shell

## Execution Prompt

Build a native operator tool that is clear, dense, and trustworthy. The user should be able to understand why a candidate is being surfaced and what happened after acting on it.

## Constraints

- the shell must consume runtime contracts instead of redefining them
- provenance and confidence must stay visible
- feedback capture must map back to the runtime feedback-event contract
- the shell must remain macOS-native in behavior and density

## Acceptance Checks

- the shell can show evidence context and frontier candidates
- the shell can show provenance, status, and ranking-relevant metadata
- the shell can capture feedback events through the runtime contract
- the shell builds locally and reflects the documented design-system baseline

## Objective

Add the first product adapter for `{reply}`, including the omnichannel conversation context contract that supplies `{trinity}` with timeline-aware evidence and consumes surfaced reply candidates.

## Unified Context

`{reply}` is expected to be the first production embedding. It already owns omnichannel conversation history and contact-level timeline context. `{trinity}` should not rebuild that product domain. Instead, it needs a clean adapter seam so `{reply}` can provide:

- unified contact timeline context,
- source-platform metadata,
- message and draft events,
- feedback outcomes.

This issue is where the first product embedding becomes concrete without turning the runtime core into `{reply}` internals.

## Problem

Without a product adapter contract:

- `{reply}` integration will happen through ad hoc assumptions,
- omnichannel context will leak into core workflow code,
- feedback events will be harder to align with real user actions,
- the first production embedding will be harder to reproduce and test.

## Goal

Create a clean product adapter seam for `{reply}` that gives `{trinity}` high-quality timeline context while preserving repository boundaries.

## Scope
### In Scope

- `{reply}` adapter interface
- omnichannel evidence mapping rules
- timeline snapshot and source metadata contract
- reply candidate delivery contract
- feedback-event mapping back from `{reply}` actions into `{trinity}` runtime events

### Out of Scope

- implementing all of `{reply}` inside this repository
- moving omnichannel sync logic into `{trinity}` core
- hosted deployment concerns

## Execution Prompt

Treat `{reply}` as the first embedding, not the whole platform. The adapter should make integration clean and reproducible without letting product details collapse runtime boundaries.

## Constraints

- the product adapter must stay outside core workflow code
- omnichannel context must remain explicit and auditable

- feedback actions must map back to runtime lineage cleanly

## Objective

Prove one real local-first reply-drafting cycle in which `{trinity}` consumes omnichannel conversation context, generates candidates, surfaces a frontier, captures operator action, and preserves the resulting feedback lineage.

## Unified Context

A workflow platform is only real once it completes one honest end-to-end cycle. For `{trinity}`, the first proof should happen through the `{reply}` embedding because that is the most concrete immediate product use. The proof needs to show that the workflow can run locally, surface useful drafts, and capture outcome signals without relying on invisible manual glue.

## Problem

Without a real proof cycle:

- the repository may look complete while still hiding integration gaps,
- local-first claims will remain theoretical,
- feedback and frontier contracts will not be pressure-tested,
- `{train}` will have no stable runtime target to optimize later.

## Goal

Demonstrate one real reply-drafting cycle through the full `{trinity}` workflow with durable evidence, frontier, and feedback artifacts.

## Scope
### In Scope

- one local ingestion-to-frontier cycle
- one surfaced reply-drafting interaction
- feedback capture from the operator action path
- proof notes and reproducible evidence of what happened

### Out of Scope

- full product rollout
- large-scale benchmark optimization
- hosted infrastructure

## Execution Prompt

Run an honest local proof. If gaps appear in contracts, surface them directly instead of papering over them with manual steps.

## Constraints

- the proof must be local-first in reality
- the proof must use the documented workflow contract, not one-off scripts that bypass it
- the proof must leave behind enough evidence that another developer can repeat it
- the proof should validate reply drafting through `{reply}` without moving product logic into `{trinity}` core

## Acceptance Checks

- one real conversation context can enter the workflow through the documented adapter path
- the workflow can surface a frontier of reply candidates locally
- one operator action can be captured as a feedback event with lineage
- the proof is documented and reproducible enough for another developer to replay

## Dependencies

- #5
- #6
- #7
- #8
- #9
- #10

## Risks

- a fake proof built from shortcuts will create false confidence
- the first honest proof may expose boundary problems; that is expected and useful

## Delivery Artifact

## Objective

Define and implement the explicit seams through which `{train}` can optimize parts of `{trinity}` without collapsing runtime and optimizer responsibilities into one codebase.

## Unified Context

The long-term architecture depends on a clean division of labor:

- `{trinity}` runs the workflow,
- `{train}` improves components of the workflow.

That relationship cannot remain an informal idea. The runtime needs explicit optimization seams around components such as retrieval, generation policy, refinement policy, evaluation policy, ranking, and abstention behavior.

## Problem

Without explicit optimization seams:

- `{train}` will not know what unit it is improving,
- runtime code will become harder to evolve without breaking future optimization work,
- teams will be tempted to move optimizer behavior directly into `{trinity}`,
- reproducibility between runtime and optimization loops will suffer.

## Goal

Define the component boundaries, artifacts, and evaluation surfaces that let `{train}` improve `{trinity}` responsibly.

## Scope
### In Scope

- identification of optimizable components
- mutable artifact strategy for workflow components
- evaluation surface contracts for optimizer use
- replay and artifact expectations for future optimization work
- documentation of runtime versus optimizer responsibilities

### Out of Scope

- implementing full `{train}` projects in this repository
- moving ratchet or experiment-ledger logic into `{trinity}`
- making the runtime depend on the optimizer to function

Design the seams so `{train}` can improve the runtime later without owning or redefining it.

## Constraints

## Objective

Make every additional generation, refinement, and evaluation pass re-anchor on canonical evidence and thread state so later workflow steps cannot drift into self-referential behavior.

## Unified Context

`{trinity}` now has a working candidate pipeline, frontier selection, reply runtime traces, and feedback application. What it still does not guarantee is that repeated processing stays grounded in canonical evidence instead of recursively amplifying prior model output. The OpenMythos mirror reinforced the same core lesson in a different domain: repeated computation only remains trustworthy when the original signal is explicitly re-injected every pass.

## Problem

Without explicit evidence re-anchoring:

- refinement passes can optimize against previous drafts instead of source truth,
- evaluator decisions can converge on polished but weakly grounded candidates,
- downstream feedback can reinforce artifacts of earlier model behavior rather than the evidence base,
- replayability will appear deterministic while still drifting semantically.

## Goal

Define and implement an evidence-anchoring contract for any multi-pass runtime behavior so repeated workflow execution preserves provenance and source grounding.

## Scope
### In Scope

- canonical re-anchoring rules for generator, refiner, and evaluator passes
- explicit handling of thread snapshots and evidence-unit refresh rules
- tests proving repeated passes still preserve source alignment
- auditable trace fields showing what evidence was re-consulted on each pass

### Out of Scope

- new model architectures
- distributed persistence changes
- product-specific UI presentation

## Execution Prompt

Treat evidence re-anchoring as a trust boundary. Reprocessing must improve the system's judgment without weakening its tie to the underlying record.

## Constraints

- evidence provenance must remain inspectable after any number of passes
- repeated execution must not require hidden prompt state
- replay behavior must remain deterministic for a fixed snapshot and policy version
- product adapters must consume the contract rather than redefine it

## Acceptance Checks

- repeated generation, refinement, and evaluation passes explicitly re-consult canonical evidence
